The angular size of the event horizon is given as \(\theta = 10^{-17}\) degrees at a distance \(d = 10^{10}\) parsecs. To find the entropy, we first convert the angular size to radians and the distance to meters:

\[
\theta_{\text{rad}} = 10^{-17} \times \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 1.745 \times 10^{-19} \text{ rad}
\]
\[
d = 10^{10} \text{ pc} \times 3.086 \times 10^{16} \text{ m/pc} \approx 3.086 \times 10^{26} \text{ m}
\]

The angular size corresponds to the angular diameter of the event horizon, so the Schwarzschild radius is:
\[
R_S = \frac{\theta_{\text{rad}} d}{2} \approx 2.69 \times 10^7 \text{ m}
\]

The area of the event horizon is:
\[
A = 4\pi R_S^2 \approx 9.11 \times 10^{15} \text{ m}^2
\]

The Bekenstein–Hawking entropy is:
\[
S = \frac{k_B A}{4 l_P^2}
\]
where \(k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K}\) and the Planck length squared is \(l_P^2 \approx 2.61 \times 10^{-70} \text{ m}^2\). Substituting the values:
\[
S \approx \frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 9.11 \times 10^{15}}{4 \times 2.61 \times 10^{-70}} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{62} \text{ J/K}
\]

The order of magnitude is \(10^{62} \text{ J/K}\). (Common mistakes include forgetting to convert degrees to radians, which gives \(10^{65}\), and then doubling that, which gives \(10^{66}\).)

Answer: A
